![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14255499/assets/38883c7cc4bfe8c9ecccadfcc2d0c75ff66f79b19ff697c15ddbe53f4c63dbab.png)

We need to create a cylindrical tin with a lid using $96\pi \,{in}^{2}$ of sheet metal. What is the largest possible volume of the cylinder?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $96\pi \,{in}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+2\pi {r}^{2}=96\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =96\pi -2\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{96\pi -2\pi {r}^{2}}{2\pi r} \\ h & =\frac{48-{r}^{2}}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}\times \frac{48-{r}^{2}}{r} \\ V(r) & =(48r-{r}^{3})\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=(48-3{r}^{2})\pi .
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ (48-3{r}^{2})\pi  & =0 \\ 48 & =3{r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =16 \\ r & =4\,\text{in}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=4$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=-6\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(4)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=4$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=4\,\text{in}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume, we substitute $r=4\,\text{in}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V(4) & =(48(4)-(4)^{3})\pi  \\  & =(192-64)\pi  \\  & =128\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the largest possible volume of the cylinder is $V=128\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}.$

questions.problem:
A manufacturer wishes to build a cylindrical tank with a base and a lid. The tank must have an exact volume of $6\pi \,{ft}^{3}.$
To make the tank, the manufacturer uses two materials:

- a metal sheet that costs $\$4$ per ${ft}^{2}$ for the lateral surface,

- a metal sheet that costs $\$1.50$ per ${ft}^{2}$ for the base and lid.

What is the radius $r$ of the tank that gives the smallest possible manufacturing cost? Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}} $\text{ft}$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a picture of a cylinder. Let $r$ be the radius, and $h$ the height.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14255499/assets/55de2c06ea57724513e450cbf49a0477d63cd75bac601d5d95f0ba7e366852ff.png)

We wish to minimize the manufacturing cost. We can express the manufacturing cost $C$ in terms of $r$ and $h$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(2\pi rh)\cdot 4+(2\pi {r}^{2})\cdot 1.5 \\  & =8\pi rh+3\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the volume is fixed at $6\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
6\pi =\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
h=\frac{6}{{r}^{2}}.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C(r) & =8\pi r(\frac{6}{{r}^{2}})+3\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{48\pi }{r}+3\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to minimize $C,$ so we need to differentiate $C$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{C}^{′}(r)=-\frac{48\pi }{{r}^{2}}+6\pi r.
$$

 

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ -\frac{48\pi }{{r}^{2}}+6\pi r & =0 \\ 6\pi r & =\frac{48\pi }{{r}^{2}} \\ 6\pi {r}^{3} & =48\pi  \\ {r}^{3} & =8 \\ r & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\ r & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a calculator, we can verify that if $r<2$ then ${C}^{′}(r)<0,$ and if $r>2$ then ${C}^{′}(r)>0,$ which means that the stationary point $r=2$ is indeed a minimum of $C(r).$

Therefore, the tank with the smallest manufacturing cost has radius $r=2\,\text{ft}.$

{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}$

First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $12\pi \,{cm}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}=12\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =12\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{6}{r}-\frac{r}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}(\frac{6}{r}-\frac{r}{2}) \\ V(r) & =(6r-\frac{{r}^{3}}{2})\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=(6-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2})\pi .
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ (6-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2})\pi  & =0 \\ 6 & =\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =4 \\ r & =2\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=2$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(2)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=2$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=2\,\text{cm}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume ${V}_{\text{max}},$ we substitute $r=2\,\text{cm}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{max}}=V(2) & =(6(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{3})\pi  \\  & =(12-4)\pi  \\  & =8\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$
